title: Common Redis Performance Pitfalls
description: Identify and fix the most frequent mistakes that cause Redis to underperform or fail under load.

data.text: Redis is fast by design, but it can still be slowed down by bad patterns. A single KEYS pattern scan, an oversized hash, or a missing index can turn a sub-millisecond cache into a multi-second blocking operation. These pitfalls are often invisible until production traffic reveals them, so knowing what to avoid is as important as knowing how to optimize.

KEYS pattern scans every key in the database sequentially. It runs in O(N) time, where N is the total number of keys. On a Redis instance with millions of keys, KEYS can block for seconds or even minutes, blocking all other clients. Never use KEYS in application code. Use SCAN for safe iteration, or maintain secondary indexes with sets.

data.title: Production Anti-Pattern
data.text: If you see KEYS in a code review, replace it immediately. SCAN is safe for production. If you need fast lookups by pattern, build a secondary index with Redis sets at write time.

A single hash with millions of fields causes Redis to allocate large contiguous memory blocks and slows down operations like HGETALL. Similarly, a list with millions of elements forces Redis to traverse the entire list for LRANGE operations. If your data structures grow without bound, you are setting yourself up for latency spikes.

data.title: Avoiding unbounded growth with bucketing (Node.js)

data.text: Blocking Commands in the Event Loop

Commands like LRANGE 0 -1 on a massive list, HGETALL on a huge hash, or ZRANGE on a sorted set with millions of members block the Redis event loop. While the command runs, no other client can be served. This is the single most common cause of latency spikes in production Redis. Always bound your range queries.

data.text: In C#, blocking calls like .Wait() or .Result on async Redis operations can cause thread-pool starvation. StackExchange.Redis is fully async, and blocking it blocks threads. Always use async/await. Also, avoid creating a new ConnectionMultiplexer per request — it is a connection pool, not a disposable connection.

data.title: Avoid blocking async calls (C#)

items: Replace KEYS with SCAN or secondary indexes
Bound all range queries with LIMIT or time buckets
Use async/await exclusively in C# async Redis code
Set maxmemory-policy before running out of memory
data.title: Quick fix checklist

items.question: How do I find blocking commands in my application?
items.answer: Enable SLOWLOG GET 128 to see recently executed slow commands. Use MONITOR for real-time tracing, but only briefly — MONITOR adds overhead.

items.question: Is SCAN safe for production?
items.answer: Yes. SCAN iterates safely using a cursor, returning only a small batch of keys per call. It does not block other clients, though individual calls still have some cost.

items.question: What is the best eviction policy for a cache?
items.answer: allkeys-lru evicts the least recently used keys from all data, which is ideal for caches. Use volatile-lru only if you need to protect keys without TTL from eviction.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: NEVER use KEYS in production — SCAN is safe
Bound range queries to prevent blocking the event loop
Use async/await in C# to avoid thread-pool starvation
Share ConnectionMultiplexer instead of creating new ones
Configure LRU eviction before you need it
data.takeaway: Performance pitfalls are often simple mistakes with huge consequences. The safest approach is to assume every command can block, every structure can grow unbounded, and every async call should be awaited.
